title: Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinates
lead: Polar coordinates extend into space in two ways: cylindrical coordinates add the height z, and spherical coordinates use a distance and two angles. This section converts points and equations among the three systems, names the surfaces each coordinate sweeps out when held constant, and chooses the system that suits a problem.
objectives: Convert from cylindrical to rectangular coordinates.
Convert from rectangular to cylindrical coordinates.
Convert from spherical to rectangular coordinates.
Convert from rectangular to spherical coordinates.
summary_html:
• In the cylindrical coordinate system, a point in space is represented by the ordered triple $(r,\ktheta ,z),$ where $(r,\ktheta )$ represents the polar coordinates of the point’s projection in the xy-plane and $z$ represents the point’s projection onto the z-axis.
  • To convert a point from cylindrical coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, use equations $x=r\;\cos \ktheta ,$ $y=r\;\sin \ktheta ,$ and $z=z.$
  • To convert a point from Cartesian coordinates to cylindrical coordinates, use equations $r^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2},$ $\tan \ktheta =\frac{y}{x},$ and $z=z.$
  • In the spherical coordinate system, a point $P$ in space is represented by the ordered triple $(ρ,\ktheta ,\kphi),$ where $ρ$ is the distance between $P$ and the origin $(ρ\ne 0),$ $\ktheta$ is the same angle used to describe the location in cylindrical coordinates, and $\kphi$ is the angle formed by the positive z-axis and line segment $\overline{OP},$ where $O$ is the origin and $0\le \kphi\le \pi .$
  • To convert a point from spherical coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, use equations $x=ρ\;\sin \kphi\;\cos \ktheta ,$ $y=ρ\;\sin \kphi\;\sin \ktheta ,$ and $z=ρ\;\cos \kphi.$
  • To convert a point from Cartesian coordinates to spherical coordinates, use equations ${ρ}^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2},$ $\tan \ktheta =\frac{y}{x},$ and $\kphi=\operatorname{arccos}(\frac{z}{\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}}).$
  • To convert a point from spherical coordinates to cylindrical coordinates, use equations $r=ρ\;\sin \kphi,$ $\ktheta =\ktheta ,$ and $z=ρ\;\cos \kphi.$
  • To convert a point from cylindrical coordinates to spherical coordinates, use equations $ρ=\sqrt{r^{2}+z^{2}},$ $\ktheta =\ktheta ,$ and $\kphi=\operatorname{arccos}(\frac{z}{\sqrt{r^{2}+z^{2}}}).$

The (Figure 12.90) The Pythagorean theorem provides equation r²=x²+y². Right-triangle relationships tell us that x=r cos θ , y=r sin θ , and tan θ =y/x. (Figure 12.93) The projection of the point in the xy-plane is 4 units from the origin. The line from the origin to the point’s projection forms an angle of 2π/3 with the positive x-axis. The point lies 2 units below the xy-plane.

(Figure 12.91) In rectangular coordinates, (a) surfaces of the form x=c are planes parallel to the yz-plane, (b) surfaces of the form y=c are planes parallel to the xz-plane, and (c) surfaces of the form z=c are planes parallel to the xy-plane. (Figure 12.92) In cylindrical coordinates, (a) surfaces of the form r=c are vertical cylinders of radius c, (b) surfaces of the form θ =c are half-planes at angle c from the x-axis, and (c) surfaces of the form z=c are planes parallel to the xy-plane. (Figure 12.99) In spherical coordinates, surfaces of the form ρ=c are spheres of radius ρ (a), surfaces of the form θ =c are half-planes at an angle θ from the x-axis (b), and surfaces of the form ϕ=c are half-cones at an angle ϕ from the z-axis (c).
In polar coordinates, the equation θ =π /4 describes the ray extending diagonally through the first quadrant. In three dimensions, this same equation describes a half-plane.

exercises.prompt: Point $R$ has cylindrical coordinates $(5,\frac{\pi}{6},4)$. Plot $R$ and describe its location in space using rectangular, or Cartesian, coordinates.

answer.solution: The rectangular coordinates of the point are $(\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{5}{2},4).$
answer.hint: The first two components match the polar coordinates of the point in the xy-plane.

exercises.prompt: Convert point $(-8,8,-7)$ from Cartesian coordinates to cylindrical coordinates.
Describe the surface with cylindrical equation $r=6.$

answer.solution: This surface is a cylinder with radius $6.$
answer.hint: The $\theta$ and $z$ components of points on the surface can take any value.

exercises.prompt: Plot the point with spherical coordinates $(2,-\frac{5\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{6})$ and describe its location in both rectangular and cylindrical coordinates.

answer.solution: Cartesian: $(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\sqrt{3}),$ cylindrical: $(1,-\frac{5\pi}{6},\sqrt{3})$
answer.hint: Converting the coordinates first may help to find the location of the point in space more easily.

exercises.prompt: Describe the surfaces defined by the following equations. a. $ρ=13$ b. $\theta =\frac{2\pi}{3}$ c. $φ=\frac{\pi}{4}$

answer.solution: a. This is the set of all points $13$ units from the origin. This set forms a sphere with radius $13.$ b. This set of points forms a half plane. The angle between the half plane and the positive x-axis is $\theta =\frac{2\pi}{3}.$ c. Let $P$ be a point on this surface. The position vector of this point forms an angle of $φ=\frac{\pi}{4}$ with the positive z-axis, which means that points closer to the origin are closer to the axis. These points form a half-cone.
answer.hint: Think about what each component represents and what it means to hold that component constant.

exercises.prompt: Sydney, Australia is at $34^{\circ}\text{S}$ and $151^{\circ}\text{E}.$ Express Sydney’s location in spherical coordinates.

answer.hint: Because Sydney lies south of the equator, we need to add $90^{\circ}$ to find the angle measured from the positive z-axis.

exercises.prompt:
Which coordinate system is most appropriate for creating a star map, as viewed from Earth (see the following figure)?

How should we orient the coordinate axes?

answer.solution: Spherical coordinates with the origin located at the center of the earth, the z-axis aligned with the North Pole, and the x-axis aligned with the prime meridian
answer.hint: What kinds of symmetry are present in this situation?
